chapter_theme: The Azhuganni's songs end in two voices. Seven more cries to the Mother (1514 to 1520) confess that love's play, forgetting her, begging from the base and a lost practice have ruined the poet. Then the refrain changes to ஆத்தாடி (1521 to 1529) and the poet speaks as a woman to her friend, telling how one came as guru, burned the six supports, the fifty-one letters and the tattvas, and left her heart a bare void with the Lord mingled in it like light in a ruby; these stanzas are shared, nearly word for word, with Pattinathar's second Arutpulambal.
structure_note: 1514 to 1520 keep the four-line form with the என் கண்ணம்மா refrain and a closing question. 1521 to 1529 are couplets split by the ஆத்தாடி refrain: the guru's coming (1521, 1522), the burning of the body's parts (1523, 1524), worship given up and the void (1525, 1526), the indwelling Lord (1527), and the poet's fall and the ignorance of others (1528, 1529). The final stanza is a fragment.

1514.reading: Taking my mother as lasting and my fathers as my equals, I came to the play of delusion and my mind was dazed; if I left the play of delusion and the daze lifted, would my mother be lasting, or my fathers equal, my Mother?
1514.nuance: மாயக் கலவி is the union of maya, read plainly as sexual play and in the cipher as the soul's mixing with the world. The verse makes the family itself a product of the daze: with the daze gone, no mother is permanent and no father is a peer. தந்தையர் in the plural is odd; it may mean elders.

1515.reading: A thief without fear, a sinner without anyone, a cruel one without love who goes and tells the heart's secrets, a ganja-drunkard: before the ruin is done, would it not do to rule him, saying 'do not fear', my Mother?
1515.nuance: The one abused is most likely the poet's own mind, named thief, sinner and drunkard; the plea is that the Mother govern it before it does harm. கஞ்சா வெறியன் is a rare literal reference to the drug among the Siddhars. Some read the thief as the breath that will not stay.

1516.reading: Forgetting you I became a worm-eaten tree; those who forget themselves have no mother or father; if, not forgetting myself, I had a mother, would I not live joined to you without forgetting you, my Mother?
1516.nuance: Forgetting the Mother and forgetting oneself are made one act, and knowing oneself is the condition for having a mother at all. உளுத்த மரம், a tree rotted from within, is the body without that remembrance.

1517.reading: In the seat of the body I bought the root of fragrance, put on the ornaments of maya and took the goods that live; before I had examined them at the testing-ghat, how did the magic scroll fall into my lap, my Mother?
1517.nuance: The verse is a merchant's tale in cipher: buying goods in the body's town, adorning oneself with maya, and the ஆயத்துறை, the toll-house where goods are checked. The சுருளோலை, the rolled palm leaf, is read as the writ of fate or Yama's summons arriving before the examination is done. Nothing in it is certain.

1518.reading: Having pricked the picture and drawn the statue, without showing the beam I became the town's public hall; if I showed the beam and became the hall, would the picture be anything else, and would the statue not fall apart, my Mother?
1518.nuance: சித்திரம், சிலை, உத்திரம் and அம்பலம் are terms of building: the picture and image are the body, the உத்திரம் the roof-beam, read as the central channel or the supporting truth, and the ambalam the open hall, Siva's dancing place. The verse seems to say that once the hidden beam is shown, picture and statue are seen as nothing in themselves.

1519.reading: Going to the base and holding out my hand for goods, I show all my teeth and stare about; will you not give me wealth, my Mother, so that I need not show my teeth, stare about or go to the base?
1519.nuance: பொருள் is both goods and the true substance; the poet asks the Mother for the one so he may stop begging for the other. The grimace of the beggar, teeth bared and eyes wide, is the humiliation the Kural's chapter on begging describes.

1520.reading: Struck by the cut wheel I gave what wealth I had and stood beaten before ten million men; will you not, instead of my standing beaten, cut away my disease before the ten million and, opening your eyes, show me the open space, my Mother?
1520.nuance: வெட்டுண்ட சக்கரம் is unclear: a broken wheel, perhaps the wheel of births, or a cut chakra. கோடி மனு is a crowd of men, or ten million births. வெளி காட்டாயோ, show the open space, asks for the Siddhar's vision of the void.

1521.reading: I became the servant of the five-handed god, friend, asking to receive grace; one came unbearably, friend, and showed me the self's own form.
1521.nuance: The bow to Ganesa opens the sequence as it opens Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2. தற்சொரூபம், the self's own form, is read either as the guru's own form or as the poet's true self; Pattinathar's text has தன்சொரூபம், his own.

1522.reading: To cut off the plundering birth, friend, he took the guru's form; to cut off the thieving senses, friend, he came as the cause.
1522.nuance: கொள்ளை பிறப்பு and கள்ளப் புலன்: birth is a robber and the senses are thieves, and the guru is the Lord's answer to both. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:2 with the refrain.

1523.reading: The six supports, friend, and the fifty-one letters, the whole fort of deceit, friend, he burned so that no fault remained.
1523.nuance: The six adharas and the fifty-one letters of the alphabet, which the mantra-yoga builds the body from, are here a சூதான கோட்டை, a fort of trickery, and the guru burns the whole structure rather than ascending it.

1524.reading: The five beginning with speech, friend, I saw die and fall; all the tattvas, friend, lost their heads and burned.
1524.nuance: வாகாதி ஐவர் is வாக்காதி ஐவர், the five organs of action beginning with speech. The stanza splices two of Pattinathar's couplets (Arutpulambal 2:4 and 2:8), taking one line from each.

1525.reading: Without bathing her in water, friend, without plucking flowers to strew, my heart became a bare void, friend; I do not see the state in which it stood.
1525.nuance: The rites of image worship are simply dropped, not argued against, and what remains is வெறும் பாழ், an emptiness the speaker cannot locate or describe. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:43.

1526.reading: Having sung and studied, friend, without adorning her with many flowers, without running about, friend, I lost my form.
1526.nuance: ஓடித் திரியாமல் is the pilgrim's running from shrine to shrine, given up; உருக்கெட்டு is plainly 'I was undone' and in the cipher 'I lost form'. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:44.

1527.reading: He stayed mingled in me, friend, like the light within a ruby; he is the greatness, friend, that the devotees who cherish and worship him do not speak of.
1527.nuance: Light in a ruby is indwelling without mixture: the gem is not the light, yet the light is nowhere else. பேசாப் பெருமை is a greatness known and not spoken. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:45.

1528.reading: My mind confused, friend, I went by the way of the puffed grain; not knowing how to set it, friend, I fell headlong into the pit.
1528.nuance: பொரிவழி, the way of பொரி, is obscure: puffed rice scattered as an offering, or a path that bursts. பாழி may be a pit, a cave or a monastery; the plain sense is a fall through confusion, and it has no doublet in Pattinathar.

1529.reading: The ancient thing that has no arising and no dissolving, friend, they do not know.
1529.nuance: தோற்றம் ஒடுக்கம் இல்லா தொல்பொருள் names the Supreme by negation, as what neither appears nor is withdrawn. The stanza breaks off after its first couplet.

links.note: The same stanza as the opening of Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2, with the ஆத்தாடி refrain inserted: the bow to Ganesa and the one who came and showed his form. The Azhuganni reads தற்சொரூபம், Pattinathar தன்சொரூபம்.
The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:2 word for word: the Lord takes the guru's form to cut off birth and the thieving senses.

The second line, he came as the cause to cut off the thieving senses, recurs in a stanza of the 1887 recension of Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2 whose first line calls him the one inside the inner and without town or name.
Arutpulambal 2:3 with the refrain; both burn the six supports and the fifty-one letters as a fort of deceit.
The second line, all the tattvas lost their heads and burned, is Arutpulambal 2:4's second line; the Azhuganni drops Pattinathar's first line about the tattvas breeding disturbance.
The first line, seeing the five beginning with speech die and fall, is Arutpulambal 2:8's second line, spliced here to the tattva line of 2:4.
Arutpulambal 2:43 with the refrain: worship dropped and the heart a bare void.
Arutpulambal 2:44 with the refrain: having sung and studied, the form lost without flowers and running about.
Arutpulambal 2:45 with the refrain: the light within the ruby and the greatness the devotees do not speak.

Both set the Lord as a ruby within: Tirumular's ruby sunk in the visible body, whose worth none knows until seen, and the Azhuganni's Lord mingled like the light within a ruby, a greatness the devotees do not speak of.

The Kural begs all who beg not to beg of those who conceal; the Azhuganni, baring his teeth to the base for goods, asks the Mother for wealth so that he need not go to them. Both find the shame of begging in the giver as much as in the asking.

Tirumular praises the worship that rises above the six-and-six supports as a splendour gained through Nandi's teaching; the Azhuganni's guru burns the six supports and the fifty-one letters as a fort of deceit. On the reading that the adharas are the ladder of yoga, one text climbs it and the other burns it.

Tirumular says those who recite, worship and heap flowers without love have minds like a stone in a mossy pond; the Azhuganni, having sung and studied, drops the flowers and the pilgrim's running and loses his form. Both set the outward rite below what happens in the heart.

source_issues: 1514 and 1516 line 4 read கண்னம்மா for கண்ணம்மா; 1518 line 4 likewise.
1519 line 3 reads காட்டமல் and line 4 போகமல், each missing a vowel sign (காட்டாமல், போகாமல்).

1521 to 1527 are near-doublets of Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2 (seq 506 to 509, 513, 548 to 550) with the ஆத்தாடி refrain inserted; 1524 splices lines from two of Pattinathar's couplets. Which poet the shared lines belong to is open.
1529 is numbered u1 in the corpus and is a fragment: only the first couplet survives, marked by an ellipsis.
